title: Pediatric Respiratory Distress: Children Compensate Until They Do Not
bottomLine: In children, increased work of breathing often appears before hypotension or arrest. Watch respiratory rate, retractions, nasal flaring, grunting, air entry, color, feeding, mental status and fatigue; decreasing effort in a previously struggling child can mean exhaustion, not improvement.
recognize: Infants may show poor feeding, head bobbing, retractions or apnea
Stridor suggests upper-airway obstruction; wheeze suggests lower-airway narrowing
Grunting can signal attempts to maintain end-expiratory pressure
Bradycardia is a late sign of hypoxia in children
assess: Airway position/patency, respiratory effort and rate, breath sounds/air entry, SpO2, color and mental status
Hydration and ability to feed
Compare current behavior with developmental baseline
actions: Position airway and minimize agitation when upper-airway obstruction is possible
Give oxygen/airway support and disease-specific therapy as ordered
Escalate fatigue, poor air entry, cyanosis, apnea, bradycardia or altered responsiveness
diagnostics: Clinical assessment drives initial stabilization; tests are cause-specific and should not delay airway support
medicationSafety: Weight-based respiratory medications require current weight and maximum-dose checks
Sedating medications can worsen respiratory compromise
teaching: Caregivers should seek urgent care for retractions, grunting, blue color, apnea, inability to feed or marked sleepiness
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN pediatric practice depends on setting. Focused respiratory assessment, ordered therapy and immediate escalation are core responsibilities.
examTrap: Interpreting a slowing respiratory rate as improvement when the child is becoming drowsy and retracting less because of fatigue.
oneLinePearl: A tired child with less respiratory effort may be closer to failure, not recovery.

title: Bronchiolitis: Suction, Hydration, Oxygen When Needed
bottomLine: Most bronchiolitis care is supportive: nasal suctioning, hydration/feeding support and oxygen for persistent hypoxemia. Routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics and chest radiographs are not automatically indicated in an otherwise typical uncomplicated case.
recognize: Infant with viral prodrome followed by cough, tachypnea, wheeze/crackles, retractions and feeding difficulty
Young age, prematurity and cardiopulmonary disease increase risk
Apnea can occur in young infants
assess: Work of breathing, SpO2, nasal obstruction and air entry
Feeding amount, wet diapers and hydration
Apnea, fatigue and ability to maintain oral intake
actions: Gentle nasal suction especially before feeding
Small frequent feeds or enteral/IV hydration when oral intake inadequate
Oxygen when persistent hypoxemia meets the treatment plan
Escalate apnea or respiratory failure
diagnostics: Diagnosis is usually clinical; routine viral testing, imaging and labs are not needed in every typical case
medicationSafety: Do not give antibiotics for viral bronchiolitis without bacterial indication
Routine albuterol/steroid therapy is not recommended for typical bronchiolitis
teaching: Nasal suction, hydration and return precautions; avoid smoke exposure
Explain that cough/wheeze can persist while breathing and feeding gradually improve
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN supports respiratory/hydration monitoring and ordered supportive treatment and recognizes when the child needs higher-acuity care.
examTrap: Expecting routine antibiotics or corticosteroids because wheezing is present.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiolitis is usually suction + fluids + oxygen if needed, not a medication parade.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics Bronchiolitis Clinical Practice Guideline

title: Croup: Barking Cough, Stridor, Keep the Child Calm
bottomLine: Croup causes upper-airway swelling with barking cough and stridor. Minimize agitation, give dexamethasone as ordered, use nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe stridor and observe for recurrence. Stridor at rest, severe retractions, cyanosis, fatigue or reduced air entry requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor
Symptoms often worsen at night
Drooling, tripod position, toxic appearance or inability to swallow suggests a different dangerous airway process
assess: Stridor at rest versus only with agitation
Retractions, air entry, color, SpO2, mental status and hydration
Keep invasive throat examination to a minimum when dangerous upper-airway obstruction is suspected
actions: Keep caregiver and child together/calm when possible
Give dexamethasone and nebulized epinephrine according to severity/order
Provide oxygen without forcing a mask on a frightened child if other safe methods work
Prepare for advanced airway support if deteriorating
diagnostics: Typical croup is a clinical diagnosis and does not routinely require neck radiographs
medicationSafety: Nebulized epinephrine can produce transient improvement, so observation after treatment is needed
Antibiotics are not used for uncomplicated viral croup
teaching: Return for stridor at rest, retractions, blue color, inability to drink, drooling or marked lethargy
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers ordered therapies and monitors airway response. Deteriorating upper-airway obstruction requires immediate pediatric/airway escalation.
examTrap: Using a tongue depressor to aggressively inspect the throat of a toxic drooling child with possible epiglottic obstruction.
oneLinePearl: Croup: calm child, steroid, epinephrine if stridor is significant, watch the airway.

title: Pediatric Dehydration: Perfusion and Weight Matter More Than Tears Alone
bottomLine: Children can lose fluid quickly. Assess behavior, heart rate, perfusion, mucous membranes, tears, urine output and weight change; use oral rehydration for mild/moderate dehydration when the child can drink, and isotonic IV resuscitation for shock or inability to tolerate enteral fluids.
recognize: Reduced urine/wet diapers, dry mouth, fewer tears, tachycardia, delayed cap refill, lethargy
Infants may have a sunken fontanelle but this is not the only severity marker
Hypotension is late in pediatric shock
assess: Current/pre-illness weight if known, intake/output and losses
Heart rate, cap refill, pulses, mental status and respiratory pattern
Sodium, glucose, renal tests when moderate/severe or atypical
actions: Use oral rehydration solution in frequent small amounts when appropriate
Continue age-appropriate feeding/breastfeeding as tolerated
Give ordered isotonic IV bolus for hypovolemic shock and reassess after each bolus
Replace ongoing losses
diagnostics: Laboratory tests are not required for every mild gastroenteritis case; they are useful when severe, prolonged, very young, or electrolyte disorder is suspected
medicationSafety: Avoid plain water, soda or sports drinks as primary rehydration for infants/young children with significant gastroenteritis
Antidiarrheals are not routinely appropriate in young children
teaching: Use oral rehydration solution, small frequent volumes and monitor wet diapers/urination; seek care for lethargy, no urine, blood, persistent vomiting or breathing difficulty
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs hydration/perfusion reassessment and ordered fluid therapy. Weight-based IV plans and severe electrolyte correction are provider-directed.
examTrap: Waiting for hypotension before recognizing significant pediatric dehydration/shock.
oneLinePearl: Kids compensate until late—watch perfusion, behavior and urine early.
sourceBasis: AAP/CDC pediatric acute gastroenteritis and oral rehydration principles

title: Fever in a Young Infant: Age Changes the Risk
bottomLine: A documented fever in an infant under about 60 days requires age- and risk-stratified medical evaluation because invasive bacterial infection can occur despite a well appearance. Do not dismiss fever because the infant is feeding or looks comfortable at the moment.
recognize: Young infants may have few localizing symptoms
Poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, apnea, color change or hypothermia can also signal infection
Risk and workup differ substantially by exact age in days
assess: Exact age, measured temperature method/value, appearance, feeding and urine
Respiratory effort, perfusion, fontanelle/neuro status and skin
Birth history and maternal/perinatal infection risks
actions: Notify pediatric clinician promptly and follow age-specific febrile-infant pathway
Obtain ordered urine/blood/CSF studies using correct technique
Give empiric antibiotics when indicated after cultures without harmful delay
diagnostics: Urinalysis/culture is a common component; blood inflammatory markers and lumbar puncture depend on exact age/risk
Clinical pathways apply to well-appearing term infants and have exclusions
medicationSafety: Acetaminophen does not replace infection evaluation in a young infant
Ibuprofen is not routinely used in young infants under 6 months without clinician direction
teaching: Caregivers of young infants should seek prompt medical evaluation for fever according to age-specific instructions rather than waiting for additional symptoms
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN recognizes the high-risk age group, obtains accurate temperature and focused assessment, collects ordered specimens and escalates. Workup disposition is pediatric-provider directed.
examTrap: Giving an antipyretic and sending a 3-week-old febrile infant home because the baby looks well afterward.
oneLinePearl: Young infant + fever = age-specific serious-infection pathway.
sourceBasis: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8 to 60 Days Old

title: Kawasaki Disease: Fever Plus Inflammation With Coronary Risk
bottomLine: Kawasaki disease is prolonged pediatric fever with mucocutaneous inflammation and risk of coronary artery aneurysm. Persistent fever plus conjunctival injection, oral changes, rash, extremity changes or cervical node findings requires pediatric evaluation; treatment with IVIG and aspirin under specialist direction reduces coronary complications.
recognize: Persistent fever
Bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis
Strawberry/red cracked lips or oral erythema
Polymorphous rash, hand/foot edema or later peeling, cervical lymphadenopathy
Incomplete Kawasaki can occur
assess: Fever duration, hydration/irritability and cardiac symptoms
CBC, inflammatory markers, liver/urine and echocardiography as ordered
Monitor for hypotension/shock and myocarditis
actions: Administer IVIG and aspirin as ordered
Monitor cardiac status and fever recurrence
Arrange echocardiographic/cardiology follow-up
diagnostics: Diagnosis is clinical with supportive labs/echo; no single test rules it in or out
medicationSafety: Aspirin use in Kawasaki is a specialist-directed exception to routine pediatric avoidance
Live-vaccine timing may need adjustment after IVIG
teaching: Keep cardiology follow-up and follow vaccine timing instructions after IVIG
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN recognizes the pattern, gives ordered IVIG/aspirin in appropriate setting, monitors reaction/cardiac symptoms and escalates.
examTrap: Refusing prescribed aspirin because aspirin is generally avoided in children, without recognizing the Kawasaki treatment exception.
oneLinePearl: Kawasaki is a fever-plus-inflammation disease with coronary consequences.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association Kawasaki Disease Scientific Statement

title: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic Spell: Calm, Knee-Chest, Oxygen, Escalate
bottomLine: A hypercyanotic spell in Tetralogy of Fallot causes sudden worsening right-to-left shunting, often with crying, feeding or exertion. Calm the child, use knee-chest positioning, provide oxygen and ordered medication/fluids, and escalate if cyanosis or distress persists.
recognize: Sudden deep cyanosis, tachypnea, irritability or syncope
Infants may instinctively draw knees up; older children may squat
Prolonged spells can cause neurologic injury or arrest
assess: Color, respiratory effort, SpO2 trend, heart rate, responsiveness
Trigger and duration
Hydration and signs of severe hypoxemia
actions: Knee-chest position and calm/comfort
Give oxygen and ordered morphine/beta blocker/fluids according to emergency plan
Activate pediatric/cardiac emergency support for persistent spell
diagnostics: Known congenital anatomy guides diagnosis; acute stabilization takes priority over testing
medicationSafety: Morphine and beta blockers require respiratory/hemodynamic monitoring
Avoid causing additional agitation during interventions
redFlags: Failure to improve with initial measures
teaching: Caregivers of children with TOF should know individualized spell actions and when to call EMS
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN follows the child's congenital-heart emergency plan and escalates promptly. Advanced medication/resuscitation depends on setting and protocol.
examTrap: Laying the child flat and forcing a painful procedure while the cyanosis worsens from agitation.
oneLinePearl: Tet spell: calm, knees to chest, oxygen, help.
sourceBasis: AAP/AHA congenital heart disease care principles

title: Febrile Seizure: Protect the Child, Then Evaluate the Fever
bottomLine: A simple febrile seizure is brief, generalized and occurs in the typical age range without prior neurologic cause, but the first priority during any seizure is safety, airway positioning and timing. Prolonged, focal, recurrent, meningitic or persistently altered presentations require more urgent evaluation.
recognize: Simple febrile seizure is generally generalized, short and single in 24 hours
Complex features include prolonged duration, focality or recurrence
Antipyretics improve comfort but do not reliably prevent future febrile seizures
assess: Time seizure, breathing/color and postictal recovery
Temperature and source of fever
Assess meningitis signs, age, immunization and baseline neurologic history
actions: Protect from injury, side-position when possible, nothing in mouth
If seizure is prolonged, use rescue benzodiazepine per protocol
Evaluate fever source and serious infection risk
diagnostics: Routine EEG/neuroimaging is not needed after every simple febrile seizure
Lumbar puncture is selected based on meningitis risk and clinical context
medicationSafety: Antipyretics are for comfort, not guaranteed seizure prevention
Benzodiazepines can depress respiration
teaching: Place child on side, protect from injury, time seizure, do not put objects in mouth, and know EMS thresholds
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN provides seizure safety, rescue medication under protocol and focused postictal assessment and escalates complex features.
examTrap: Using ice baths or alcohol rubs to rapidly lower fever to prevent another seizure.
oneLinePearl: Febrile seizure: safe seizure care first; fever evaluation second.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Pediatrics Febrile Seizure Clinical Guidance

title: Intussusception: Episodic Pain Can Progress to Ischemia
bottomLine: Intussusception classically causes sudden episodic severe abdominal pain with periods of relative calm; vomiting, lethargy and later bloody mucus stool can occur. Keep the child NPO, support fluids, and prepare for ultrasound plus air/contrast enema reduction unless perforation/peritonitis requires surgery.
recognize: Intermittent drawing up of legs/crying episodes
Vomiting and lethargy may be prominent
Currant-jelly stool is a later finding and not required
Peritonitis indicates ischemia/perforation
assess: Pain pattern, vomiting/stool, hydration and perfusion
Abdominal tenderness/distention/mass
Watch for fever, rigidity and shock
actions: NPO and IV fluids as ordered
Prepare for ultrasound and therapeutic pneumatic/hydrostatic enema
Escalate peritonitis or unstable child for surgery
diagnostics: Ultrasound is highly useful; enema can diagnose and reduce
Do not wait for currant-jelly stool before acting
medicationSafety: Analgesia is appropriate while maintaining reassessment
Avoid laxatives/enemas outside the controlled reduction procedure
teaching: After reduction, report recurrent episodic pain/vomiting because recurrence can occur
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN supports NPO/fluids and pre/post reduction assessment. Enema reduction and surgery are specialized procedures.
examTrap: Waiting for the classic currant-jelly stool before notifying the provider.
oneLinePearl: Intussusception: episodic pain + vomiting/lethargy; jelly stool is late.

title: Pyloric Stenosis: Projectile Vomiting, Dehydration, Alkalosis
bottomLine: Infant hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting, dehydration and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Correct fluid and electrolyte deficits before pyloromyotomy; surgery is urgent but not performed before major dehydration/electrolyte disturbance is stabilized.
recognize: Hungry infant with forceful nonbilious vomiting after feeds
Poor weight gain, fewer wet diapers and dehydration
Olive-shaped mass or visible peristalsis may be present but are not required
assess: Hydration, weight, intake/output and vomiting characteristics
Electrolytes and acid-base status
Differentiate bilious vomiting, which suggests obstruction distal to stomach and is a different emergency
actions: NPO and IV isotonic fluid/electrolyte correction as ordered
NG decompression only if ordered/indicated
Prepare for pyloromyotomy after metabolic stabilization
diagnostics: Ultrasound is the usual diagnostic test
Electrolytes can show hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
medicationSafety: Correct potassium only after adequate urine output and according to order
Do not treat vomiting with routine antiemetics instead of correcting the obstruction
teaching: Postoperative feeds are advanced according to the surgical plan; small residual vomiting can occur early but persistent worsening needs reassessment
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN tracks hydration/electrolyte response and pre/post-op care. Surgical timing is pediatric/surgical-team directed.
examTrap: Rushing the infant directly to surgery before correcting significant dehydration and alkalosis.
oneLinePearl: Pyloric stenosis: nonbilious projectile vomiting—fluids first, surgery after stabilization.

title: Pediatric Medication Dosing: Kilograms, Maximum Dose, Decimal Safety
bottomLine: Pediatric doses are commonly weight-based, so verify an accurate current weight in kilograms, prescribed mg/kg dose, dosing frequency, concentration, route and maximum adult/single/day dose. Use leading zeros and never trailing zeros; question any dose that exceeds safe limits even if the arithmetic itself is correct.
recognize: Confusing pounds with kilograms can create a more than twofold dosing error
Liquid concentrations can vary between products
Weight-based math must still respect dose caps and organ function
assess: Current measured kg weight and allergies
Renal/hepatic function and age-specific contraindications
Exact medication concentration and device
actions: Calculate mg dose first, then convert to volume
Use an independent double-check for high-alert medications when required
Clarify unsafe or ambiguous decimal/concentration orders before administration
diagnostics: Therapeutic drug monitoring is medication-specific and especially important for selected narrow-therapeutic-index agents
medicationSafety: Write 0.5 mg, never .5 mg; write 5 mg, never 5.0 mg
Use oral syringes rather than household spoons for liquid medicines
Do not exceed maximum dose simply because mg/kg calculation is higher
redFlags: Dose calculated from pounds as though kilograms
teaching: Caregivers should know the medication name, exact dose and mL amount, frequency and measuring device
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN must independently verify safe pediatric medication administration within scope and question unsafe orders rather than assuming the prescriber already checked the math.
examTrap: Giving the calculated mg/kg dose even though it exceeds the medication's established maximum dose.
oneLinePearl: Peds meds: kg first, mg second, mL third, max dose always.

title: Growth and Development: Safety Changes With the Stage
bottomLine: Developmental assessment looks at trajectory across motor, language, cognitive and social domains—not one milestone in isolation. Prevention teaching must match developmental ability: safe sleep/feeding in infancy, choking/poison/fall prevention in toddlers, helmets/restraints/water safety in childhood and confidential risk screening in adolescence.
recognize: Development varies, but loss of previously acquired skills is always concerning
Premature infants may use corrected age for early developmental interpretation
Caregiver concern is clinically meaningful and should not be dismissed
assess: Milestone trajectory, growth pattern, school/function and family context
Vision/hearing and communication
Developmental screening at recommended visits and autism screening according to pediatric schedule
actions: Refer for early intervention/developmental evaluation when screening or concerns indicate
Use age-appropriate injury prevention and car-seat guidance
Provide adolescent privacy within legal/safety limits
diagnostics: Screening identifies risk; it is not itself a developmental diagnosis
medicationSafety: Keep medications and toxic products locked and use child-resistant packaging, recognizing it is not childproof
teaching: Use the current AAP Bright Futures preventive schedule and CDC developmental resources; tailor safety teaching to the child's actual stage
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN contributes observations, screening data and family teaching and reports developmental regression or safety concerns. Diagnosis/referral decisions follow the pediatric team.
examTrap: Labeling a child delayed from one missed milestone without assessing the overall developmental trajectory—or ignoring regression because milestones vary.
oneLinePearl: Milestones are a trajectory; regression is a red flag.
